\noindent *Yellow-highlighted values in this document mark thresholds,
anchors, counts and other numerical choices that should be verified
against the source paper, the LEPA reference, or the raw data before
publication.*

# Purpose and scope

This pipeline takes raw macroinvertebrate sampling data from
Lithuanian rivers, harmonises taxonomy through a project-specific
Operational Taxalist (OTL), and recalculates the multimetric
**Lithuanian River Macroinvertebrate Index (LRMI)** under the EU Water
Framework Directive (WFD). The recalculated values are then compared
against the LEPA-published EQRs and EQCs for a curated subset of sites
to test whether OTL standardisation materially alters the assessment.

The pipeline is implemented as seven core R scripts in `Scripts/`
(numbered 1–7) plus three diagnostic scripts (8–10) and a
self-contained HTML decision tree. Inputs sit in `Inputs/`; every
output is written to `Outputs/` prefixed with the **producing
script's number** so the mapping is one-to-one (e.g. script 6 writes
`Outputs/6_LRMI_with_comparison.xlsx`).

**Scope:** all analyses from Stage 4 onwards are restricted to
\hl{2014–2022}. Pre-2014 LEPA EQRs were calculated using the older
single-DSFI assessment rather than the LRMI, and including them in
the comparison would conflate methodological era with taxonomic
standardisation effects (see Findings, §10).

# Workflow at a glance

| Stage | Script | Purpose |
|------:|--------|---------|
| 1 | `1_generate_decision_tree_html_v17.R` | Render decision-tree HTML from editable text blocks |
| 2 | `2_OTU_assignment_v22.R` | Apply decision tree to assign an OTU to every taxon |
| 3 | `3_DSFI_calculator_v15.R` | Compute the Danish Stream Fauna Index (DSFI) per sample |
| 4 | `4_calculation_of_taxonomic_indices.R` | Compute BMWP / ASPT, group richness/abundance, compound indices |
| 5 | `5_merge_indices_and_metadata.R` | Join DSFI + taxonomic indices + site metadata |
| 6 | `6_calculate_LRMI.R` | Calculate the LRMI and ecological-quality class per site-year |
| 7 | `7_comparing_eqrs.R` | Compare LRMI / class against LEPA's published values |
| 8 | `8_DEP_OTL_vs_validated.R` (diagnostic) | Test whether residual LEPA-vs-LT differences trace to #DEP |
| 9 | `9_per_metric_diagnostic.R` (diagnostic) | Per-metric breakdown for class-mismatch site-years |
| 10 | `10_lepa_per_metric_comparison.R` (diagnostic) | Direct head-to-head against LEPA's published per-metric EQRs |

# Stage 1 — Decision-tree design (Script 1)

## Inputs to the design

A Lithuanian aquatic-invertebrate species list was compiled from
national literature and validated against the GBIF and Molluscabase
taxonomic backbones. Four specialists (\hl{2} current EPA biomonitoring
identifiers, \hl{1} former identifier now calculating national EQRs,
\hl{1} independent researcher) were asked to state, for each species,
the **coarsest** taxonomic level they could reliably identify it to
(species / genus / subfamily / family / order / subclass / class /
phylum).

## Three synchronised representations

To keep the rules transparent and reviewable, the decision tree is
maintained in three locked-step representations:

- `Outputs/1_OTL_decision_tree_v17_machine_readable.md` — the
  canonical human-readable specification (plain text,
  version-controlled).
- `Outputs/1_OTL_decision_tree_v17.html` — visual flow-chart for
  non-technical reviewers and supplementary material.
- The R script `1_generate_decision_tree_html_v17.R` — generates the
  HTML directly from editable content blocks, so the visual document
  cannot drift out of sync with the rule text it represents.

Any rule change is made in the `.md` (authoritative) and the R
generator script in parallel; sourcing the generator re-renders the
HTML. The four-phase logic below is the content these three
representations agree on.

## OTU assignment rules

The OTU for each taxon is determined by a four-phase decision tree
(see `Outputs/1_OTL_decision_tree_v17.html` for the full visual version):

**Phase 1 — Preparation.** Validate names, flag exclusions from EQR
using the `excluded_taxa` sheet as the source of truth.

**Phase 2 — Forced-level overrides.** A small number of groups receive
a fixed OTU level regardless of specialist agreement. These taxa
**skip Phases 3 and 4** entirely. The overrides are:

| Group | Forced level | EQR? | Reason |
|-------|--------------|------|--------|
| Entirely excluded groups (all families excluded) | group level | excluded | non-target / non-aquatic / non-macroscopic |
| Oligochaeta (Naididae) | family | included | DSFI uses Naididae at family (IG6) |
| Other Oligochaeta | subclass | included | difficult routine identification |
| Neuroptera (Osmylidae, Sisyridae) | family | included | specialist order-level was too coarse |
| Stenostomidae | phylum | excluded | order is taxonomically unstable |
| All other excluded-from-EQR taxa | family | excluded | natural ceiling at family |

Entirely excluded groups:

- Phyla: Porifera, Cnidaria, Nematoda, Nematomorpha, Nemertea, Bryozoa
- Classes: Polychaeta, Arachnida, Collembola, Maxillopoda, Branchiopoda
- Orders: Stylommatophora, Dolichomicrostomida, Prolecithophora, Rhabdocoela, Anostraca

**Phase 3 — 100\% specialist agreement.** For each remaining
species-level taxon, the OTU is set to the **coarsest** level reported
by any of the four specialists (i.e. the level all four can reach).

**Phase 4 — Metric compliance.** If the Phase-3 level is coarser than
the minimum required by any downstream metric (DSFI, BMWP, etc.), the
OTU is overridden to the minimum required level. Overrides are
documented row-by-row in the output trace.

## Truly-aquatic rule for higher-level entries

Order-and-above entries are retained for EQR calculation only for
**truly aquatic** groups: Bivalvia (class); Plecoptera,
Ephemeroptera, Odonata, Megaloptera, Trichoptera (orders). All other
order+ entries are excluded from EQR (they may include terrestrial
representatives).

# Stage 2 — OTU assignment (Script 2)

`2_OTU_assignment_v22.R` implements the decision tree above against
the project's three reference sheets:

- `Specialist_taxalist` — one row per validated species, with each
  specialist's reported identification level.
- `OTL_final` — the full universe of taxa (species, genera, families
  and higher-level entries).
- `excluded_taxa` — the source of truth for which taxa are excluded
  from EQR calculations (entirely-excluded groups + individually
  excluded families/species).

The script outputs an Excel workbook with three sheets:

1. `OTL_final_with_OTU` — every row of `OTL_final` annotated with its
   assigned OTU name, OTU level, metric group, and EQR-exclusion flag.
2. `decision_tree_trace` — full per-taxon explanation of which phase
   triggered, what the agreement level was, and whether a metric
   override was applied. This is the audit trail for the supplementary
   material.
3. `hierarchical_OTL` — a parallel taxalist with fallback entries at
   every level from phylum down to species, so damaged or juvenile
   specimens identifiable only to family or order still have a valid
   OTU.

## Data-quality guard

After reading the input sheets, the script warns when a name appears
in one sheet but not another. This was added after discovering that a
typo (`Aelosoma hemprichi` in Specialist\_taxalist vs
`Aeolosoma hemprichii` in `excluded_taxa`) was silently breaking the
class-level Polychaeta exclusion.

Output: `Outputs/2_OTU_assignments_v22.xlsx`.

# Stage 3 — DSFI calculation (Script 3)

Implements Skriver et al. (2000) for each sample (site\_code × year).
The script aggregates abundances to DSFI-relevant taxa, applies
presence-threshold rules, then walks through six Indicator Groups
(IG1–IG6) to look up the DSFI value (1–7) in the published Table 2
matrix.

Key presence rules:

- Kick sample threshold: \hl{≥ 2} individuals for indicator-group
  determination (Table 2). Hand-picked sample threshold: \hl{≥ 1}.
  Diversity groups (Table 3) ignore the kick-2 filter — \hl{≥ 1}
  specimen anywhere is enough.
- Oligochaeta as a negative diversity group requires \hl{≥ 100}
  individuals in the kick sample.
- Indicator-group precluders: Asellus kick \hl{≥ 5} → IG3; Chironomus
  kick \hl{≥ 5} → IG4; Eristalini kick \hl{≥ 2} → IG6.
- IG5 lower row used when Oligochaeta kick \hl{≥ 100}.
- Simuliidae presence at IG5 requires kick \hl{≥ 25} or hand \hl{≥ 1}.

Output: `Outputs/3_DSFI_results_all_sites.xlsx` and a curated
subset of \hl{95} sites at
`Outputs/3_DSFI_results_subset.xlsx`.

# Stage 4 — Taxonomic indices (Script 4)

Computes the remaining LRMI inputs and a wider set of community
metrics from the OTL-standardised data:

- **Total richness, abundance**, Margalef / Shannon / Simpson / Pielou
  (not all used downstream; retained for completeness).
- **BMWP and ASPT** — sum of family-level sensitivity scores ÷ number
  of scoring units. Two scoring exceptions:
  - *Ancylus* sp. is scored as its own **genus-level** unit (the
    family Ancylidae was synonymised into Planorbidae but retains a
    distinct BMWP score).
  - **Oligochaeta** collapses to a single unit at score \hl{1},
    regardless of how many oligochaete OTUs are present (Naididae,
    Tubificidae, Oligochaeta Gen. sp.).
- **Group richness / abundance** for individual orders (Ephemeroptera,
  Plecoptera, Diptera, Hemiptera, Crustacea, …) and for compound
  groups (CrHi, EHP, DEP).
- **DEP** richness = number of unique Diptera families + number of
  individual E and P taxa at species level (the LEPA convention).
- **\%EHP – \%CrHi** = (Σ EHP abundances – Σ CrHi abundances) / total
  abundance.

## Hand-picked abundance treatment

Kick-sample abundances are kept as raw counts. **Hand-picked
abundances are coerced to 1 before aggregation** (presence-only) and
then summed with the kick counts within each
`site_id × year × OTL_taxonname` group. The rationale is that the
hand-picked sub-sample is qualitative — it is meant to capture taxa
that the kick sample may have missed, not to provide quantitative
density estimates. Treating hand-picked as presence/absence prevents
the qualitative supplement from skewing abundance-weighted metrics
(BMWP, \%EHP – \%CrHi, group abundances).

## Year filter

From this stage onwards the analysis is restricted to
\hl{2014–2022}. The filter is applied at the same point as the
existing taxon-exclusion filters (`NO MATCH`, `EXCLUDE`, site_code
prefix `LTR`). Rationale is in Findings (§10).

Output: `Outputs/4_calculated_taxonomic_indices.xlsx`.

# Stage 5 — Merge with site metadata (Script 5)

`5_merge_indices_and_metadata.R` joins:

1. DSFI results on `(site_id, site_code, year)`.
2. Taxonomic indices on the same key.
3. **Site metadata** (`site_meta_data` sheet) on `site_id` — static
   per-site fields: location, waterbody type, river basin, river
   type, modification state, reference-site flag.
4. **EQR metadata** (first 20 columns of `clean_macroinvertebrate_data`)
   on `(site_id, site_code, year)` — sample-level fields including
   LEPA's published EQR and EQC.

The EQR metadata sheet uses \hl{0} and `"0"` as placeholders for
"never assessed". These are converted to `NA` at load time, then
rows with NA in either EQR or EQC are dropped, so all downstream
comparisons rest on genuine LEPA assessments only.

The same \hl{2014–2022} year filter is applied to DSFI, taxonomic-
indices, and EQR-metadata inputs on read. The `site_meta_data` sheet
(static per-site fields, no year column) is not filtered.

Output: `Outputs/5_merged_indices.xlsx`.

# Stage 6 — LRMI calculation (Script 6)

Implements Sidagytė-Copilas & Arbačiauskas (2022).

## The four core metrics and their anchors

For each metric \hl{$i$}: $\text{EQR}_i = (x_i - \text{lower}_i) /
(\text{ref}_i - \text{lower}_i)$.

| Metric | Reference value | Lower anchor |
|--------|-----------------|--------------|
| DSFI | \hl{7} | \hl{1} |
| ASPT | \hl{7.0} | \hl{1.0} |
| #DEP | \hl{15} | \hl{0} |
| \%EHP – \%CrHi | \hl{0.6} | \hl{-1.0} |

## LRMI formula and our strict variant

The published method averages all four EQRs, falling back to the
remaining three if DSFI fails to key out. **We have chosen to be
stricter:** if any of the four metrics is `NA`, LRMI is `NA`. This
avoids reporting an LRMI built on only a subset of metrics.

## Clamping and rounding (project convention)

Per-metric EQRs are kept unclamped and unrounded as internal inputs.
The final LRMI is then:

1. Computed as the arithmetic mean of the four raw EQRs (`LRMI_raw`).
2. Clamped at \hl{1} (no LRMI > 1).
3. Rounded to \hl{2} decimal places (matches LEPA's reported precision).

Both `LRMI_raw` (faithful to the paper) and `LRMI` (display /
comparison value) are retained in the output.

## Ecological class boundaries

Uniform across all river types, derived from the clamped + rounded
LRMI (matches LEPA's class-from-rounded-EQR convention):

| Class | Range |
|-------|-------|
| High | LRMI \hl{≥ 0.80} |
| Good | \hl{0.60} ≤ LRMI < \hl{0.80} |
| Moderate | \hl{0.40} ≤ LRMI < \hl{0.60} |
| Poor | \hl{0.30} ≤ LRMI < \hl{0.40} |
| Bad | LRMI < \hl{0.30} |

Type-specific adjustments proposed by Sidagytė-Copilas & Arbačiauskas
(2022, their Table 5, italic rows) are **not** applied — the uniform
"Current" boundaries match LEPA's operational practice.

## Natural-waterbody scope

Only sites with `modification_state == "N"` (natural) enter the LRMI
calculation. Heavily modified or artificial waterbodies use a
different reference-condition formulation that is out of scope for
this project.

# Stage 7 — Comparison against LEPA (Script 7)

## Curated comparison subset

A \hl{27}-site subset covering a POOR → HIGH gradient was selected,
with \hl{2}–\hl{3} samples per site over \hl{2015–2022}
(\hl{82} site-years total). Sites are distributed across the four
main Lithuanian catchments and across all five WFD river types.

## What is compared

For each site-year in the subset, the LEPA-published EQR and EQC
(from the comparison input) are paired with our recalculated LRMI
and LRMI_class (from Stage 5). Comparisons include:

1. **1:1 scatterplot** of LEPA EQR vs LT-OTL LRMI, coloured by LEPA
   EQC using the WFD palette, with Pearson correlation.
2. **Bland–Altman plot** with \hl{95\%} limits of agreement
   (mean ± \hl{1.96} × SD of differences) to surface systematic bias
   or wide spread.
3. **Boxplots by river type**, with horizontal WFD class bands as
   visual context.
4. **Sample-level table** with every site-year's signed `eqr_diff`
   and a boolean `eqc_match` flag, sorted by absolute EQR difference
   so the largest discrepancies surface at the top. No banded
   categories are applied; the continuous residual is reported as-is.

## Outputs

- `Outputs/6_LRMI_with_comparison.xlsx` (from Stage 6) — all
  site-years, full metric breakdown, both raw and clamped+rounded
  LRMI. Consumed by this stage.
- `Outputs/7_sample_level_comparison.xlsx` — per-sample table
  (LEPA vs LT-OTL) for case-by-case investigation, sorted by
  absolute EQR difference.
- `Plots/Figure_1.tiff` — map of Lithuanian river sampling sites
  coloured by latest-year EQC.
- `Plots/Figure_2.tiff` (script 6) — 1:1 scatter of LEPA EQR vs
  LT-OTL EQR with WFD class bands.
- `Plots/Figure_3.tiff` (script 10) — per-metric A/B comparison panel
  (scatter on top, boxplots on bottom).

The comparison input is also year-filtered to \hl{2014–2022} at read
time, defensively (the curated subset is already 2015-2022).

# Stage 8 — Diagnostics

Two ad-hoc scripts that don't feed downstream but ground the
discussion of where LEPA-vs-LT residuals come from.

## DEP-attribution diagnostic (script 8)

Script: `8_DEP_OTL_vs_validated.R`.
Tests the hypothesis that residual LEPA-vs-LT differences come from
OTL standardisation collapsing multiple species into a single OTU,
artificially lowering the #DEP count. For every site-year, DEP is
recomputed twice — once grouped by `OTL_taxonname` (matches our
LRMI), once by `taxonname_validated` (pre-OTL). The implied LRMI
shift from any DEP difference is then compared against the actual
LEPA-vs-LT residual.

**Headline result:** the correlation between the DEP-implied LRMI
shift and the actual residual is \hl{0.17} — weak. Mean
|residual| drops only from \hl{0.0256} to \hl{0.0241} after
subtracting the DEP-implied shift. **OTL standardisation is not the
dominant source of LEPA-vs-LT residuals.**

Output: `Outputs/8_DEP_OTL_vs_validated.xlsx`.

## Per-metric diagnostic (script 9)

Script: `9_per_metric_diagnostic.R`.
For a user-supplied set of site-years (the \hl{46} sites with the
largest residuals or class-mismatches), the four per-metric EQRs are
pulled alongside their percentile rank against the full
natural-waterbody distribution. The metric with the lowest percentile
is flagged as the most-likely-culprit for each site.

**Headline result:** no single metric dominates. EHP-CrHi is the
slight leader (\hl{17 / 46} sites flag it as the lowest metric;
mean percentile \hl{32.7} vs \hl{40–42} for the others), but DSFI,
ASPT, and DEP each drag down \hl{9–10} sites. \hl{40 / 46}
residuals are positive (LEPA EQR higher than our LRMI), confirming a
small systematic downward bias on boundary-region sites; \hl{43 / 46}
have |residual| ≤ \hl{0.08}, i.e. essentially boundary near-misses.

Output: `Outputs/9_per_metric_diagnostic.xlsx`.

*Note:* this script inferred metric responsibility indirectly from
percentile rank because LEPA's per-metric EQRs were not yet
available. Script 10 (below) supersedes that indirect inference
with a direct LEPA-vs-LT comparison of the same per-metric values.

## LEPA per-metric comparison (script 10)

Script: `10_lepa_per_metric_comparison.R`.
LEPA's published per-metric EQRs (DSFI, ASPT, #DEP, \%EHP-\%CrHi)
plus the final LRMI / class are read from `Inputs/LEPA metrics.xlsx`
(82 curated sites) and joined to our LT-OTL run on `site_code`. For
each metric the script reports the per-site residual (LEPA − LT-OTL),
its mean / median / |mean|, Pearson r, and the percentage of
samples agreeing to within \hl{±0.005}.

**Outputs:**

- `Outputs/10_lepa_per_metric_comparison.xlsx` — four sheets:
  per-site residuals (`per_site`), raw summary (`summary`), and two
  publication-ready tables (`publication_distribution`,
  `publication_residuals`).
- `Plots/12_lepa_per_metric_panel.tiff` — combined A/B panel:
  five-panel scatter on top (LEPA vs LT-OTL per metric, with 1:1
  reference and per-facet Pearson r / p / n) and five-panel boxplot
  on the bottom (LEPA vs OTL distributions per metric, jittered
  points overlaid, WFD class bands on the EQR facet).

This is the definitive comparison: it lets the Discussion attribute
residuals directly to a specific metric rather than inferring it.

# Findings (use to anchor the Results / Discussion text)

These are the headline numerical results the pipeline produces. They
are the most important values to verify before publication.

1. **2013 is the outlier year, not OTL standardisation.** A
   per-year breakdown of |LEPA EQR − LT-OTL LRMI| (over \hl{1026}
   site-years with a valid LEPA EQR) shows 2013 with mean |residual|
   \hl{0.085} and median \hl{0.057}, against 2014-2022 mean
   |residual| of \hl{0.011–0.023} and median \hl{0.000–0.010}.
   Interpretation: LEPA's pre-2014 EQRs were calculated under the
   old single-DSFI assessment, not the LRMI. Filtering to
   \hl{2014–2022} produces clean comparison data.

2. **DEP is not the bias source.** Per the diagnostic in §8.1,
   DEP-implied LRMI shifts correlate only \hl{r = 0.17} with the
   actual residual. Most of the residual is not explained by OTL
   collapsing E+P species.

3. **No single metric dominates the bias on boundary sites
   (indirect inference).** Per §8.2, even the most-often-low metric
   (EHP-CrHi) accounts for only \hl{37\%} of the 46 worst sites. The
   bias is distributed across all four metrics. Note: this finding
   was derived before LEPA's per-metric EQRs were available. The
   direct head-to-head comparison in §8.3 (script 10) provides the
   definitive per-metric attribution and should be reported in
   preference once its numbers are pinned down.

4. **\hl{≈ 95\%} of LRMI-era site-years (2014-2022) agree closely
   with LEPA.** Median residual \hl{0.01}, mean |residual|
   \hl{0.014-0.023}. The remaining ~5\% are mostly small
   class-boundary near-misses.

5. **Per-metric residuals against LEPA — EHP-CrHi carries the gap.**
   Direct comparison against LEPA's published per-metric EQRs on the
   \hl{82}-site curated subset (script 10) gives:

   | Metric | n | Mean residual<br>(LEPA − LT-OTL) | Mean \|residual\| | Pearson r | \% within ±0.005 |
   |--------|--:|--------------------------------:|------------------:|----------:|----------------:|
   | DSFI | 82 | \hl{−0.008} | \hl{0.016} | \hl{0.981} | \hl{90.2\%} |
   | ASPT | 82 | \hl{+0.001} | \hl{0.005} | \hl{0.996} | \hl{68.3\%} |
   | #DEP | 82 | \hl{+0.005} | \hl{0.005} | \hl{0.998} | \hl{93.9\%} |
   | \%EHP − \%CrHi | 82 | \hl{+0.062} | \hl{0.062} | \hl{0.774} | \hl{35.4\%} |
   | LRMI (final EQR) | 82 | \hl{+0.015} | \hl{0.018} | \hl{0.991} | \hl{43.9\%} |

   **Interpretation.** Three of the four per-metric EQRs (DSFI, ASPT,
   #DEP) agree with LEPA at r ≥ \hl{0.98} and mean |residual| ≤
   \hl{0.016} — essentially identical. The residual on the final LRMI
   is driven almost entirely by **\%EHP − \%CrHi**: mean residual
   \hl{+0.062} (LEPA higher), mean |residual| \hl{0.062}, and the only
   metric with r below \hl{0.99} (r = \hl{0.774}, 35\% within ±0.005).
   The systematic positive sign means LEPA's EHP-CrHi values run
   slightly higher than ours, plausibly because the qualitative
   hand-picked count of crustaceans/hirudineans differs between the
   two pipelines (LEPA's treatment of hand-picked specimens is not
   documented in the published data dictionary).

# Decisions worth flagging in Materials & Methods

The following choices deviate from a strict reading of the cited
papers and should be stated explicitly:

1. **LRMI strict NA rule** — paper averages remaining metrics if DSFI
   fails; we set LRMI to NA. Effect: \hl{0} samples in our dataset (DSFI always keys out in our data), but worth declaring.
2. **LRMI clamped at 1 and rounded to \hl{2 dp}** — paper allows
   values > 1 (their Fig. 5). We match LEPA's reported precision and
   ceiling.
3. **Uniform class boundaries** across all river types — type-specific
   offsets proposed in the paper (Table 5 italic rows) are not used.
4. **Natural-waterbodies-only scope** — heavily modified waterbodies
   are excluded from the recalculation.
5. **Oligochaeta collapse for BMWP** — all oligochaete OTUs are pooled
   into a single scoring unit at score 1, by OTL_taxonname match
   (`Oligochaeta Gen. sp.`, `Naididae Gen. sp.`, `Tubificidae Gen. sp.`).
6. **Ancylus as a genus-level BMWP unit** — preserves the historical
   Ancylidae score distinct from Planorbidae despite the recent
   taxonomic synonymy.
7. **fwe.info comparison removed** — earlier versions of the pipeline
   compared OTL against a freshwaterecology.info standardisation; this
   has been dropped from the current paper scope.
8. **Year filter \hl{2014–2022}** — applied from Stage 4 onwards.
   LEPA's pre-2014 EQRs were not the LRMI but the older single-DSFI
   assessment, so including them in the comparison would conflate
   methodological era with taxonomic-standardisation effects
   (see Findings §10.1).
9. **Hand-picked abundance treatment** — Stage 4 coerces hand-picked
   abundances to 1 before aggregating with kick counts. The
   hand-picked sub-sample is qualitative (intended to extend the taxon
   list, not provide density estimates), so contributing it as
   presence-only prevents the qualitative supplement from biasing the
   abundance-weighted metrics.
10. **Non-indigenous species (NIMS)** — invasive taxa are not given
    any special treatment in this pipeline. The raw taxonomy is too
    unreliable for a confident NIMS flag, and the OTL collapses many
    of the most error-prone groups to coarser units anyway; any NIMS
    correction at this stage would be downstream of the very
    uncertainty it is trying to address. Sidagytė-Copilas &
    Arbačiauskas (2022) flag this as a future-work item and apply no
    NIMS correction themselves; we follow that convention.
11. **BMWP scores** — the per-family BMWP sensitivity scores are
    taken from the `BMWP_lookup` sheet in
    `Inputs/All_sites_macroinvertebrate_data_long.xlsx`, which is the
    single source of truth for the project. No external published
    table is consulted at run time.
12. **Year filter as a hard methodological cut** — the
    \hl{2014–2022} window is treated as the "operational LRMI era"
    and is a hard methodological choice. No supplementary comparison
    over the 2013 transition is reported, because the goal is a
    like-for-like comparison of OTL standardisation against LEPA's
    LRMI assessment, not a comparison spanning the change from the
    pre-2014 single-DSFI assessment.
13. **Sample-level residual reported as a continuous value** — script
    7's per-sample comparison table reports `eqr_diff` as a signed
    continuous residual and `eqc_match` as a boolean class-agreement
    flag. The earlier coarse magnitude bands (`identical` / `minor` /
    `moderate` / `large` at 0.05 and 0.10 cutoffs) have been dropped
    because the thresholds had no external anchor; the continuous
    residual plus the EQC-match flag captures the same information
    without imposing arbitrary categorical boundaries.

# Reproducibility notes

- R version: \hl{≥ 4.0.5} (matching the cited paper's environment).
- Packages: `tidyverse`, `readxl`, `writexl`, `vegan`, `reshape2`,
  `ggplot2`, `sf`, `ggrepel`, `cowplot`, `rnaturalearth`,
  `rgeoboundaries`, `ggspatial`.
- Working directory at run time: the project root containing
  `Inputs/`, `Outputs/`, `Scripts/`.
- Scripts are numbered 1–10 matching the producing stage; their
  outputs are written with the same numeric prefix in `Outputs/` (or
  `Plots/`). Older versioned scripts (`_v1`, `_v17` etc.) have been
  retired to `Backup scripts/` and are not part of the live pipeline.
- The `.gitignore` excludes `Backup scripts/`, `Literature/`, and
  Claude-related artefacts (`.claude/`, `CLAUDE.md`) from version
  control.
